record.field: Send confirmations directly to banks to verify cash balances, interest rates, and any restrictions on the cash.
Compare confirmed balances with recorded cash balances and investigate any discrepancies.
Obtain and review bank reconciliations for all cash accounts, ensuring they are completed and independently reviewed.
Verify the accuracy of reconciling items, such as outstanding checks and deposits in transit, and ensure that they are recorded in the appropriate period.
Obtain the year-end bank statements and a few months of subsequent statements for all cash accounts.
Scan bank statements for unusual transactions, such as large transfers or unexpected payments, and verify legitimacy.
Perform cutoff testing to ensure that cash transactions near year-end are recorded in the correct period.
Select a sample of cash receipts and cash disbursements around period-end, tracing them to supporting documentation to verify proper cutoff.
Review the composition of cash equivalents, ensuring compliance with the entity’s policies and accounting standards.
Verify valuation of cash equivalents by recalculating fair values, considering the type of cash equivalents (e.g., treasury bills, short-term investments).
For foreign currency-denominated cash accounts, verify that year-end balances are translated using the appropriate exchange rate.
Recalculate foreign currency balances and ensure gains or losses are recorded according to accounting standards.
Verify petty cash funds by physically inspecting the petty cash balance, counting the cash on hand, and reconciling it to recorded amounts.
Review petty cash vouchers for proper documentation, approval, and completeness.
Perform analytical procedures on cash balances to detect unusual fluctuations compared to prior periods.
Investigate any unexpected variances in cash balances by obtaining explanations from management and corroborating with supporting documents.
Identify any restricted cash accounts (e.g., compensating balances, collateral for loans) and assess whether they are properly classified and disclosed.
Confirm that restrictions are properly disclosed in the financial statements.
Calculate interest income on cash balances to verify accuracy.
Compare actual interest income received with expected amounts based on cash balances and applicable interest rates.
Send positive confirmations to a sample of customers to verify the existence, accuracy, and ownership of receivables.
For non-responses, consider performing alternative procedures, such as vouching to subsequent cash receipts or sales invoices.
Review cash receipts after year-end to verify the accuracy and existence of accounts receivable as of the balance sheet date.
Match cash receipts to outstanding receivables at year-end and investigate any unusual or unmatched items.
Reconcile the accounts receivable subsidiary ledger with the general ledger.
Investigate any discrepancies to ensure completeness and accuracy of recorded receivables.
Select a sample of sales transactions around period-end to verify that they are recorded in the correct accounting period.
Trace selected transactions to supporting documentation, such as shipping and delivery records.
Analyze the aged accounts receivable report to identify any overdue or slow-paying accounts.
Assess the adequacy of the allowance for doubtful accounts by considering historical collection rates, current economic conditions, and specific high-risk accounts.
Perform analytical procedures to assess the reasonableness of accounts receivable balances compared to prior periods and industry benchmarks.
Investigate any unusual trends or fluctuations by obtaining explanations from management and corroborating them with supporting documentation.
Review a sample of credit memos and adjustments issued during the period to ensure they are properly authorized and accurately recorded.
Investigate any unusual or large adjustments that may indicate revenue manipulation.
For foreign currency-denominated receivables, verify that balances are translated using the correct exchange rate as of the balance sheet date.
Recalculate foreign currency adjustments and verify gains or losses are properly recorded.
If any accounts receivable are factored, pledged, or assigned, review supporting agreements and disclosures.
Confirm that such accounts are properly valued, classified, and disclosed in the financial statements.
Review any related party receivables to ensure they are separately disclosed and properly valued.
Test for adequate approval, appropriate classification, and disclosures in the financial statements.
Reconcile the contract asset subsidiary ledger with the general ledger to ensure completeness and accuracy.
Investigate any discrepancies between the two ledgers.
Select a sample of contract asset balances and vouch them to underlying documents, such as contracts, project schedules, and performance reports.
Verify that the recorded contract asset represents work completed and not yet billed, based on contract terms.
Review calculations for the percentage of completion or other methods used to recognize revenue on a sample of contracts.
Confirm the accuracy of project completion assessments by reconciling with project budgets, cost-to-date, and milestones achieved.
Review subsequent billing records to confirm that contract assets are converted to receivables or revenue in a timely manner.
Match contract asset balances at year-end to subsequent billings and cash receipts where applicable.
Test a sample of contract asset transactions near period-end to verify that they are recorded in the correct period.
Trace transactions to underlying documentation, such as project completion records or cost-to-complete reports, to verify proper cutoff.
Evaluate the assumptions and calculations related to the cost-to-complete estimates and profit margins on a sample of ongoing projects.
Confirm that any changes in estimates or significant changes in project scope are documented, approved, and appropriately reflected in contract asset balances.
Perform analytical procedures to detect unusual trends or fluctuations in contract asset balances compared to prior periods or expectations.
Investigate any unexpected changes by obtaining explanations from management and corroborating with supporting documentation.
Review any reversals or adjustments to contract asset balances to ensure they are properly authorized, documented, and accurately recorded.
Investigate any unusual or large adjustments, such as those made for anticipated losses or contract modifications.
Review contract asset balances for any related party transactions to ensure they are disclosed and valued appropriately.
Confirm that related party contracts are recognized and measured consistently with third-party contracts.
For contract assets denominated in foreign currency, verify that they are translated using the appropriate exchange rates as of the balance sheet date.
Recalculate foreign currency adjustments and verify that any gains or losses are recorded according to accounting standards.
Confirm that the presentation and disclosure of contract assets in the financial statements meet accounting standards.
Ensure that any significant contract terms, risks, and unfulfilled performance obligations are adequately disclosed.
Send confirmations to custodians, brokers, and other counterparties to verify financial assets' existence, ownership, and balances as of the reporting date.
Compare confirmed balances with recorded balances and investigate any discrepancies.
Reconcile the subsidiary investment ledger with the general ledger, confirming completeness and accuracy.
Investigate any differences or unusual items between the subsidiary ledger and the general ledger.
For publicly traded financial assets, obtain market prices as of the balance sheet date from reliable sources to verify recorded fair values.
For non-traded or complex financial assets, review management’s valuation techniques and assumptions, or obtain independent valuation if available.
Review classification of financial assets (e.g., fair value through profit or loss, fair value through other comprehensive income, amortized cost) for compliance with accounting standards.
Ensure that gains or losses, reclassifications, and impairments are appropriately recorded and disclosed.
Assess whether there is any evidence of impairment in financial assets based on the issuer's financial health, market conditions, or other relevant factors.
Confirm that impairment losses are recognized timely and in accordance with applicable standards.
Perform analytical procedures on financial assets, comparing balances to prior periods, budgeted amounts, or market indices.
Investigate any unusual trends, significant changes, or deviations from expectations by corroborating explanations with supporting documentation.
Test transactions around the balance sheet date to ensure they are recorded in the correct period.
Review supporting documentation, such as trade confirmations and settlement statements, to confirm appropriate cutoff.
Review the recorded gains and losses for accuracy, ensuring that realized gains/losses reflect proper sale dates and unrealized gains/losses reflect correct valuation.
Verify that unrealized gains or losses are appropriately classified based on the entity’s accounting policies.
For foreign currency-denominated financial assets, verify that balances are translated at the appropriate exchange rate as of the balance sheet date.
Recalculate foreign currency adjustments and ensure that any resulting gains or losses are recorded properly.
Review the valuation, classification, and disclosures of any derivative financial instruments.
Test the fair value calculation methodology and underlying assumptions used in valuing derivatives, ensuring compliance with accounting standards.
Test interest, dividends, and other income on financial assets by comparing to contract terms, rates, or dividend announcements.
Confirm that income on financial assets is accurately calculated, recorded in the correct period, and adequately disclosed.
Confirm that financial assets are properly classified, disclosed, and presented in the financial statements per applicable standards.
Verify that significant terms, risks, and fair value hierarchy levels are adequately disclosed.
Send confirmations to counterparties for all derivative contracts to verify the existence, terms, and balances as of the reporting date.
Compare confirmation responses with recorded balances and investigate any discrepancies.
Reconcile the subsidiary ledger for derivatives with the general ledger, ensuring completeness and accuracy.
Investigate any differences or unusual items between the subsidiary ledger and the general ledger.
Obtain market data to independently verify fair values of derivatives as of the balance sheet date for exchange-traded derivatives.
For over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives, review management’s valuation methods, and consider reperforming the valuation or consulting with an independent valuation specialist if necessary.
Review documentation supporting hedge designations (e.g., fair value, cash flow, or net investment hedge) to ensure compliance with accounting standards.
Evaluate hedge effectiveness testing by reviewing supporting calculations and assumptions, ensuring that any ineffectiveness is accurately recorded.
Select a sample of derivative transactions around the balance sheet date to ensure they are recorded in the appropriate period.
Review supporting documentation, such as trade confirmations and settlement records, to verify proper cutoff.
Assess whether there is any evidence of impairment or unrealized losses on derivative instruments due to credit or other risks.
Confirm that unrealized losses are recognized timely and in accordance with applicable standards, particularly for derivatives not designated as hedges.
Review a sample of realized and unrealized gains and losses on derivatives, ensuring accuracy and proper classification in the financial statements.
Verify that realized gains and losses reflect accurate settlement amounts and that unrealized gains and losses align with fair values.
For foreign currency derivatives, confirm that balances are translated using the correct exchange rate as of the balance sheet date.
Recalculate currency gains or losses, ensuring proper treatment and recording in compliance with accounting standards.
For interest rate derivatives, confirm that valuation considers prevailing market interest rates and that changes in fair value are correctly calculated.
Verify that any interest income or expense arising from derivatives is recorded accurately.
Identify any embedded derivatives within hybrid financial instruments, ensuring they are properly separated and accounted for.
Confirm that management has assessed the need for bifurcation and that embedded derivatives are measured appropriately.
Perform analytical procedures to assess the reasonableness of derivative balances compared to prior periods, hedge objectives, or risk exposure.
Investigate any unusual trends or significant changes by obtaining explanations from management and corroborating them with documentation.
Confirm that derivative financial instruments are classified and presented correctly on the balance sheet (e.g., asset or liability) and by fair value hierarchy level.
Verify that adequate disclosures are made regarding the types of derivatives, risk exposures, hedging relationships, and significant terms.
Attend and observe the entity’s physical inventory count, ensuring proper procedures are followed, such as proper tagging, counting, and reconciliation.
Conduct test counts on a sample of inventory items and compare with the entity’s records for accuracy.
Reconcile the inventory subsidiary ledger with the general ledger, ensuring completeness and accuracy of the recorded balance.
Investigate any differences between the inventory ledger and the general ledger.
Review transactions recorded near the end of the period to ensure inventory purchases and sales are recorded in the correct period.
Select a sample of receiving and shipping documents around year-end and verify that they are recorded in the appropriate period.
For a sample of inventory items, review cost assignments to ensure consistency with the entity’s costing method (e.g., FIFO, LIFO).
Verify that costing calculations, such as cost per unit and total cost for each item, are accurate and consistent with the entity’s records.
Review management’s assessment of obsolete, damaged, or slow-moving inventory, ensuring items are appropriately written down to net realizable value.
Inspect a sample of inventory items to assess their physical condition and confirm management’s assertion on obsolescence.
Select a sample of inventory items and compare their recorded costs to their net realizable values.
Confirm that inventory is written down to net realizable value when it exceeds cost, in compliance with accounting standards.
Perform analytical procedures, such as inventory turnover ratio analysis, to assess inventory levels relative to sales and purchases.
Compare current year inventory levels and valuation adjustments with prior years to identify significant changes or unusual trends.
Select a sample of inventory transfer transactions and verify that they are recorded accurately and reflect the correct quantity, location, and item codes.
Ensure that inventory transfers between locations are properly authorized and recorded in the correct period.
Review WIP balances by tracing to supporting documentation, such as production reports or labor and material requisitions.
Recalculate costs allocated to WIP, ensuring labor, materials, and overhead are accurately assigned based on production stage.
For inventory held on consignment, confirm that it is excluded from the inventory balance and appropriately disclosed.
Obtain confirmations from consignees for inventory held at their locations to verify quantities and terms.
Review any outstanding inventory purchase commitments for disclosure and valuation implications.
Confirm that committed purchase prices are considered in inventory valuation assessments.
Verify that inventory is appropriately classified and disclosed in the financial statements, including costing methods and valuation adjustments.
Confirm disclosures regarding any significant inventory write-downs, valuation methods, and commitments or consigned inventory.
Obtain the prepayment schedule and agree it to the general ledger to ensure completeness and accuracy.
Test calculations on the schedule to verify that amounts are allocated appropriately across periods.
For significant prepayments (e.g., long-term insurance or rental contracts), obtain confirmations or review supporting agreements to verify terms and existence.
Confirm that the prepayment period aligns with contractual obligations and that costs have been recorded accurately.
Review prepayment transactions recorded near the period-end to ensure they are recorded in the correct period.
Examine supporting documentation, such as contracts or invoices, to verify that expenses are recognized over the correct timeframe.
Test the amortization of prepayments to confirm that they are expensed over the benefit period in line with accounting standards.
Select a sample of prepayments and recalculate the amortization amount for the current period, ensuring accuracy and consistency.
Identify any adjustments or reversals made to prepayments during the period and confirm that they are properly authorized and documented.
Investigate any unusual adjustments or large, unexpected reversals, and obtain explanations from management.
Perform analytical procedures, such as comparing current period prepayment balances to prior periods and investigating any significant fluctuations.
Compare prepayment balances as a percentage of total assets or expenses to industry benchmarks to identify potential misstatements.
For new prepayments acquired during the period, inspect supporting documentation (e.g., vendor invoices, contracts) to verify the initial recording and accuracy.
Confirm that these prepayments are included on the prepayment schedule and are allocated over the correct benefit period.
Review a sample of expense invoices to ensure that prepaid items have been correctly recorded as assets rather than expenses.
Trace recorded expenses to assess whether any additional prepayments should have been recorded but were not.
For foreign currency prepayments, confirm that balances are translated at the appropriate exchange rate as of the balance sheet date.
Recalculate foreign currency adjustments to verify that gains or losses are accurately recorded.
Review prepayment balances to confirm proper classification as current or non-current assets, depending on the period of benefit.
Confirm that all significant prepayments are appropriately disclosed in the financial statements according to accounting standards.
Obtain a schedule of prepaid taxes, detailing the nature of each prepaid tax (e.g., income tax, VAT) and the allocation of each payment to the relevant periods.
Reconcile the prepaid tax schedule to the general ledger, ensuring completeness and accuracy.
For significant prepaid tax items, obtain and inspect tax payment receipts, and confirm the amounts and dates of payments.
Verify that amounts recorded as prepaid tax agree with tax authority receipts and records.
Reconcile the prepaid tax balance to the latest tax return or correspondence from tax authorities, ensuring that prepaid amounts align with reported liabilities.
Confirm that any adjustments from prior tax periods are recorded accurately and reflect any additional tax due or refunds applied.
Select a sample of prepaid tax payments made close to the balance sheet date to ensure they are recorded in the appropriate period.
Inspect supporting documentation to confirm proper classification and recording in the correct fiscal period.
Test the amortization of prepaid tax balances, ensuring that prepaid amounts are expensed in the period in which they relate.
Recalculate the amortization of prepaid tax and confirm consistency with tax filing deadlines or anticipated benefits.
Perform analytical procedures by comparing the prepaid tax balance to prior periods and to expected tax rates.
Investigate significant changes or unusual trends in the prepaid tax balance and corroborate with supporting documentation.
Review the prepaid tax balances to determine if any part is refundable, especially for overpaid taxes or tax credits.
Confirm that refundable portions are accurately classified and determine if the recoverability of the prepaid balance is impaired due to a change in future taxable income.
For prepaid taxes denominated in foreign currencies, verify that amounts are translated to the reporting currency at the applicable exchange rate as of the balance sheet date.
Recalculate any foreign exchange adjustments to ensure accuracy and completeness.
Verify that prepaid taxes are correctly classified as current or non-current assets, depending on when the benefit is expected to be realized.
Ensure that adequate disclosures are made in the financial statements regarding the nature, amount, and timing of prepaid taxes.
Obtain a schedule of other current assets, detailing the nature and balances of each item, such as advances, deposits, and other receivables.
Reconcile this schedule to the general ledger to confirm completeness and accuracy.
For a sample of significant items, inspect supporting documentation (e.g., contracts, invoices, agreements) to verify existence, ownership, and terms of other current assets.
Confirm that amounts recorded are accurate and match supporting documentation.
Review transactions recorded near the period-end to ensure they are recorded in the correct period.
Verify that any receipts or disbursements related to these assets were appropriately recorded in the period to which they pertain.
Review the valuation basis of each category of other current assets, ensuring that they are recorded at realizable value.
For assets with indicators of impairment, such as aged advances or deposits unlikely to be recovered, confirm that provisions have been recorded in line with accounting standards.
For items such as advances to suppliers or other receivables, assess the likelihood of recovery by reviewing subsequent transactions and payment history.
Inspect any provisions for non-collectable balances and verify that they are reasonable and supported by management's assessment.
Perform analytical procedures to assess the reasonableness of other current assets by comparing current period balances to prior periods and investigating any significant changes.
Compare balances of other current assets as a percentage of total assets or working capital with industry benchmarks to identify any unusual trends.
For items classified as prepayments or deposits, confirm that they are being amortized or expensed over the period of benefit.
Recalculate amortization for prepaid items and ensure they are recorded accurately and systematically.
For other current assets denominated in foreign currencies, verify that amounts are translated to the reporting currency at the appropriate exchange rate as of the balance sheet date.
Recalculate any currency translation adjustments to ensure they are accurate and consistent.
Verify that other current assets are correctly classified in the balance sheet, ensuring only short-term items expected to be realized within the next 12 months are included.
Ensure adequate disclosures are made regarding the nature, composition, and any provisions or impairments related to other current assets.
Obtain a schedule of non-trade receivables, detailing the nature, balances, and terms of each receivable (e.g., employee advances, loans).
Reconcile this schedule to the general ledger to ensure completeness and accuracy.
For significant non-trade receivables, inspect supporting documentation, such as loan agreements or employee advance forms, to verify the existence, terms, and accuracy of recorded amounts.
Confirm that amounts recorded as non-trade receivables agree with supporting documentation.
Review transactions recorded near the period-end to ensure they are recorded in the correct period.
Inspect supporting documentation to confirm that any receipts or repayments are properly classified and recorded in the correct period.
Review the valuation of non-trade receivables to ensure they are recorded at realizable value, considering any indicators of impairment.
Test management’s assessment of collectability by reviewing any provisions for doubtful accounts or adjustments for impaired amounts.
For non-trade receivables due from employees, related parties, or tax authorities, review subsequent repayments or settlements to assess recoverability.
For aged or overdue receivables, confirm that management has appropriately assessed the likelihood of collection and recorded necessary provisions.
For non-trade receivables that accrue interest (e.g., loans to employees or related parties), confirm that interest income is accurately calculated and recorded.
Recalculate a sample of interest accruals to ensure they are in line with the terms of the agreement and properly recorded.
Perform analytical procedures to assess the reasonableness of non-trade receivables by comparing current period balances to prior periods and investigating any significant changes.
Compare the balance as a percentage of total assets or working capital with industry benchmarks to identify any unusual trends or growth in receivables.
For non-trade receivables due from related parties, review board approvals and confirm that terms are consistent with market rates.
Ensure that receivables from related parties are appropriately classified and disclosed in the financial statements.
For non-trade receivables denominated in foreign currencies, verify that amounts are translated to the reporting currency at the applicable exchange rate as of the balance sheet date.
Recalculate foreign currency adjustments to ensure accuracy.
Verify that non-trade receivables are classified correctly on the balance sheet, distinguishing between current and non-current assets.
Ensure adequate disclosures in the financial statements regarding the nature, terms, provisions for doubtful accounts, and related party receivables.
Obtain a detailed schedule of investments in associates, including the ownership percentage, carrying value, and reconciliation of the investment account for the period.
Reconcile the schedule to the general ledger, ensuring completeness and accuracy.
Verify the initial investment amount by inspecting supporting documentation, such as purchase agreements or contracts.
Confirm that the initial cost of the investment was recorded accurately and is consistent with the transaction documentation.
Obtain the most recent audited financial statements of the associate and review them to confirm the accuracy of the share of profits/losses recorded.
Recalculate the investor’s share of profit or loss based on the associate’s financial performance and confirm that it matches the recorded amount.
Review adjustments recorded under the equity method, including the share of the associate’s profits/losses and dividends received.
For each adjustment, ensure that the calculations are accurate based on the investor’s percentage ownership and that entries are recorded correctly.
Review transactions recorded near the balance sheet date to ensure they are recorded in the correct period.
Verify that any changes in ownership or transactions affecting the investment in the associate are recorded accurately.
Review for any indicators of impairment in the investment, such as significant losses, adverse market conditions, or decline in the associate’s net assets.
If impairment is identified, test management’s impairment calculations and confirm they are in line with applicable accounting standards.
For investments in associates denominated in foreign currencies, confirm that amounts are translated into the reporting currency at the appropriate exchange rate as of the balance sheet date.
Recalculate any foreign currency adjustments to verify accuracy and compliance with accounting policies.
For dividends received from associates, inspect documentation such as dividend declarations and payment receipts to confirm existence and accuracy.
Verify that dividend income is correctly recorded as a reduction in the carrying amount of the investment, per equity method guidelines.
For changes in the ownership percentage of the associate, confirm that they are accurately reflected in the investment schedule and general ledger.
Review any documentation related to changes in ownership, and ensure that the impact of changes on the investment valuation is correctly recorded.
Perform an analytical review of the investment balance by comparing it to prior periods and investigating any significant changes.
Evaluate trends in the associate’s performance metrics and consider whether adjustments or impairment indicators exist based on this analysis.
Verify that the investment in associate is appropriately classified on the balance sheet and presented as a non-current asset.
Confirm that disclosures are made in accordance with accounting standards, including information on ownership percentage, dividends, significant transactions, and any impairment losses.
Obtain a schedule detailing each joint venture, including ownership percentage, carrying value, and a reconciliation of the investment account for the period.
Reconcile the schedule to the general ledger, ensuring completeness and accuracy.
Inspect supporting documentation, such as joint venture agreements, to verify the initial cost of the investment.
Confirm that the initial investment cost recorded is accurate and matches supporting documentation.
Obtain the latest audited financial statements of the joint venture to verify the accuracy of the share of profits or losses recorded.
Recalculate the entity’s share of the joint venture’s profit or loss, ensuring it is based on the ownership percentage and accurately recorded.
For joint ventures accounted under the equity method, verify adjustments for the share of profits or losses and dividends received.

For joint ventures accounted under proportionate consolidation, confirm that the appropriate share of joint venture assets, liabilities, income, and expenses is included in the entity’s financial statements.
Review transactions recorded near the period-end to ensure they are recorded in the correct period.
Inspect supporting documentation to confirm that any changes in ownership or other material transactions are recorded accurately and in the correct period.
Assess the joint venture for any indicators of impairment, such as continued losses or declining financial performance.
If impairment indicators exist, review management’s impairment calculations and ensure they are reasonable and comply with accounting standards.
For joint ventures denominated in foreign currencies, confirm that amounts are translated to the reporting currency at the appropriate exchange rate as of the balance sheet date.
Recalculate any currency translation adjustments to verify accuracy and consistency with accounting policies.
Inspect documentation such as dividend declarations and receipts to verify any dividend income from the joint venture.
Ensure dividend income is correctly recorded and any reduction in the investment’s carrying value is in accordance with accounting standards.
Confirm that any transactions between the entity and the joint venture are properly authorized, documented, and disclosed.
Ensure that terms of related party transactions are fair and consistent with market rates, if applicable.
For any contributions or withdrawals made to or from the joint venture during the period, inspect supporting documentation to confirm the accuracy and timing of these transactions.
Ensure that contributions or withdrawals are recorded appropriately in line with the joint venture agreement.
Perform an analytical review by comparing the balance of the joint venture investment to prior periods and investigating any significant changes.
Assess whether the investment value appears reasonable in relation to the financial performance of the joint venture and industry norms.
Verify that the investment in the joint venture is appropriately classified as a non-current asset and accurately presented on the balance sheet.
Ensure adequate disclosures, including ownership percentage, share of profits/losses, dividends, impairment, and material transactions with the joint venture.
Obtain a detailed schedule of deferred tax assets, including the underlying temporary differences, tax losses, and credits carried forward.
Reconcile the schedule to the general ledger to confirm completeness and accuracy.
For a sample of temporary differences, inspect supporting documentation to verify that differences are correctly identified and accurately calculated.
Confirm that the temporary differences align with tax laws and relate to deductible amounts for which future tax benefits are likely to be realized.
Review the tax rates used in DTA calculations and verify that they are based on enacted tax rates expected to apply when the temporary differences are realized.
Test whether these tax rates are correctly applied to calculate the deferred tax assets.
Recalculate a sample of deferred tax assets by applying the correct tax rates to the temporary differences to verify the accuracy of the amounts recorded.
Confirm that the calculations align with the applicable tax regulations and entity-specific tax rates.
Review management’s assessment of the need for valuation allowances on deferred tax assets.
Inspect forecasts, budgets, and other evidence that supports management’s expectation of future taxable income, to assess whether DTAs are likely to be realized.
Review transactions and changes in temporary differences recorded near the period-end to ensure they are recorded in the correct period.
Verify that adjustments to DTAs are recorded promptly in the financial statements.
Review recent tax law changes that may affect deferred tax assets, including changes in tax rates or allowable deductions.
Test management’s calculation adjustments in response to these tax law changes and ensure they are reflected accurately in DTA balances.
Assess the likelihood of future taxable income to support the recoverability of DTAs, especially for loss carryforwards or credits.
For DTAs with a low probability of realization, verify that management has recorded appropriate valuation allowances.
For deferred tax assets denominated in foreign currencies, verify that amounts are translated into the reporting currency at the correct exchange rate as of the balance sheet date.
Recalculate any foreign currency adjustments to confirm accuracy.
Perform an analytical review of DTA balances, comparing current and prior year balances and investigating any significant changes.
Consider economic conditions and industry trends that could impact future taxable income and the realizability of deferred tax assets.
Confirm that deferred tax assets are classified correctly on the balance sheet as non-current assets.
Verify adequate disclosures, including the nature of temporary differences, loss carryforwards, valuation allowances, and any limitations on realization.
Obtain the detailed fixed asset register, including descriptions, locations, acquisition costs, accumulated depreciation, and net book values.
Reconcile the register to the general ledger to confirm accuracy and completeness.
Select a sample of additions from the fixed asset register and inspect supporting documentation, such as purchase invoices, approvals, and contracts.
Verify that each addition is recorded at cost, correctly classified, and authorized per company policy.
Select a sample of disposals and inspect documentation such as sale agreements, disposal authorizations, and evidence of cash receipts.
Confirm that disposed assets are removed from the fixed asset register, and any resulting gain or loss on disposal is accurately calculated and recorded.
Select a sample of assets and verify the accuracy of the depreciation calculations, including the method, useful life, and residual value applied.
Recalculate depreciation for selected assets and confirm consistency with the company's depreciation policies.
Review indicators of impairment, such as underutilization, technological obsolescence, or physical damage.
For assets identified with potential impairment, inspect management’s impairment tests and assumptions, ensuring adjustments are recorded correctly if impairment is required.
Perform a physical inspection of a sample of fixed assets to confirm their existence and consistency with the fixed asset register.
Ensure that assets are appropriately tagged or identified and located as per the register.
Confirm that the capitalization policy is consistently applied by reviewing a sample of acquisitions around the capitalization threshold.
Verify that only expenditures that meet the capitalization criteria are added to the fixed asset register, while repairs and maintenance are expensed.
For assets under construction, verify the amounts capitalized by inspecting construction contracts, work orders, and payment invoices.
Confirm that CIP balances are transferred to the appropriate asset category upon completion and that depreciation begins in accordance with policy.
Review fixed asset additions and disposals around the period-end to confirm proper cutoff.
Inspect invoices, authorizations, or sale agreements to ensure transactions are recorded in the correct period.
For assets that are revalued, review management’s revaluation documentation, including the basis for fair value determinations and assumptions used.
Confirm that any revaluation gains or losses are recorded accurately and in compliance with accounting standards.
Perform an analytical review by comparing current period asset additions, disposals, and depreciation expense with prior periods and budgeted amounts.
Investigate any significant or unusual changes and obtain explanations from management.
Verify that fixed assets are classified and presented correctly in the balance sheet as non-current assets.

Confirm that the disclosures in the financial statements comply with accounting standards, including asset classes, useful lives, depreciation methods, revaluation adjustments, and impairment details.
Obtain a schedule of right-of-use assets that includes each lease’s acquisition date, lease term, lease payments, and net book value.
Reconcile the schedule to the general ledger and confirm completeness and accuracy.
Select a sample of ROU assets and inspect the underlying lease agreements, verifying that they meet the criteria for capitalization.
Confirm that the initial recognition of the ROU asset is based on the present value of lease payments and accurately recorded.
Select a sample of ROU assets and recalculate the amortization or depreciation expense based on the lease term and depreciation method.
Confirm that the ROU assets are depreciated consistently with the lease term and accounting policy, and verify accuracy in the calculation.
For any leases with modifications or reassessments during the period, inspect documentation for adjustments to the ROU asset and lease liability.
Confirm that adjustments are based on updated lease terms, discount rates, or payment changes, and that modifications are correctly recorded.
Review for indicators of impairment, such as reduced usage, sublease arrangements, or adverse changes in the economic environment.
Inspect management’s impairment assessment and calculations, ensuring any impairment loss is recorded accurately in the financial statements.
Review ROU asset additions, modifications, or disposals near the period-end to confirm they are recorded in the correct period.
Inspect lease commencement dates and modification dates to verify proper timing of recognition.
For leases denominated in foreign currencies, confirm that amounts are translated to the reporting currency at the correct exchange rate as of the balance sheet date.
Recalculate any currency translation adjustments to verify accuracy and compliance with accounting policy.
Review the discount rates applied in calculating the ROU asset and lease liability, ensuring that they reflect either the rate implicit in the lease or the lessee’s incremental borrowing rate.
Test a sample of leases to verify that the correct discount rate was applied at initial recognition or modification.
Perform an analytical review by comparing the current and prior year ROU asset balances, amortization, and additions/disposals to identify significant changes.
Investigate any unusual trends or changes and obtain explanations from management.
Confirm that ROU assets are presented appropriately in the balance sheet as non-current assets, separate from owned fixed assets.
Verify that disclosures comply with accounting standards, including the nature of ROU assets, amortization methods, remaining lease terms, and any impairment.
Obtain the detailed intangible asset register, including acquisition dates, useful lives, amortization methods, and carrying amounts.
Reconcile the register to the general ledger to confirm completeness and accuracy.
Select a sample of intangible asset additions and inspect supporting documentation, such as acquisition agreements, invoices, and legal filings.
Confirm that each addition is recorded at the correct acquisition cost, is properly classified, and has been authorized per company policy.
For a sample of intangible assets with finite useful lives, verify that the amortization expense has been calculated correctly and is based on the assigned useful life and method.
Recalculate the amortization for selected assets and confirm consistency with the company’s policy on amortization.
Review the indicators of impairment, such as legal challenges, reduced cash flows, or technological obsolescence.
For intangible assets with indefinite useful lives, such as goodwill, review the annual impairment test, including management’s assumptions and supporting evidence.
Confirm that any impairment losses are calculated accurately and recorded correctly.
